## Abstract

Study Objectives

Since genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of sleep phenotypes have been conducted in differing populations and definitions of sleep phenotypes vary across studies, we investigated associations between several polygenic risk scores (PRSs) and potential sleep definitions among multiethnic cohorts.

Methods

Using data from four cohorts (HCHS/SOL, ARIC, MESA, BHS, N = 16 895), we considered multiple definitions of short and long sleep, insomnia, and excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS). PRSs were developed based on summary statistics from GWAS in European ancestry individuals from the UK Biobank (UKB) and from GWAS conducted in a multiethnic population from the Million Veteran Program (MVP). Study-specific analyses estimated associations between sleep PRSs and corresponding sleep measures per 1 standard deviation increase in the PRS. Models were adjusted for age, sex, ancestral principal components, and center and race as appropriate. Results were meta-analyzed across studies.

Results

PRSs based on European ancestry UKB GWAS had statistically significant associations with multiple definitions of the corresponding sleep phenotypes. Associations that were most consistent across studies included: short sleep PRS with ≤6 hours (OR = 1.23,p = 1.80x10^{-7},p_{het} = 0.97); long sleep PRS with ≥9 hours (OR = 1.09,p = 6.76x10^{-4},p_{het} = 0.77); insomnia PRS with the Women’s Health Initiative Insomnia Rating Scale (WHIIRS) ≥10 or a subset of three questions ≥6 in ARIC (OR = 1.17,p = 5.51x10^{-10},p_{het} = 0.69); and EDS PRS with Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) ≥11 (OR = 1.23,p = 1.83x10^{-13},p_{het} = 0.83). PRSs based on multi-ancestry MVP GWAS had weaker associations compared to those based on European ancestry only.

Conclusions

By evaluating several types of sleep PRSs and sleep phenotypes, we were able to highlight which sleep PRS performed well across diverse populations and which sleep definitions better captured genetic underpinnings.

## Materials and methods

### Cohort studies

#### The Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos

The HCHS/SOL study is a longitudinal study comprising 16 415 individuals aged 18–74 years of Hispanic/Latino origin (Cuban, Puerto Rican, Dominican, Mexican, and Central/South American) [19,20]. A two-stage probability sampling design based on census-blocks groups and household addresses was employed, enrolling individuals from four geographic sites in the United States (Miami, San Diego, Chicago, and the Bronx area of New York). Individuals aged 45 to 74 years were oversampled. To account for the sampling design, sampling weights were constructed for analyses. Participants completed comprehensive clinical examinations and health questionnaires at baseline (2008–2011) and during follow-up visits (2014-2017, 2020-2024). Information on sleep [21] and genetic data were available on 12 182 individuals at baseline.

#### Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis

The MESA study is a longitudinal study comprising 6814 individuals aged 45–84 representing diverse self-described racial and ethnic backgrounds (approximately 38% of participants are White, 28% African American, 22% Hispanic, and 12% Asian) [22,23]. Participants had no known cardiovascular disease at time of enrollment and were recruited from six sites in the United States (Forsyth County NC, New York City NY, Baltimore City and County MD, St. Paul MN, Chicago IL, Los Angeles County CA). Baseline clinical examinations and health questionnaires were completed between 2000 and 2002, with multiple follow-up visits occurring between 2002 and 2024. We used data from MESA visit 5 for main analyses and data from MESA visit 4 in a sensitivity analysis since sleep questions were more thorough and similar to other studies in MESA visit 5 but MESA visit 4 had a larger sample size (5384 individuals at visit 4 and 2085 individuals at visit 5 with sleep and genetic data).

#### Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities

The ARIC study is a population-based prospective cohort study of cardiovascular disease among 15 792 individuals, predominantly European Americans and African Americans, and has been described in detail previously [24]. Participants were aged 45-64 years at baseline (1987–1989) and chosen by probability sampling from four US communities (northwestern suburbs of Minneapolis, Minnesota; Washington County, Maryland; Forsyth County, North Carolina; and Jackson, Mississippi). Several follow-up visits were conducted between baseline and the present. In 1996-1998 (visit 4), 1920 ARIC participants from the Minnesota and Maryland field centers underwent sleep assessments as part of the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) [25]. The SHHS Sleep Habits Questionnaire was used to elicit information about habitual sleep duration, insomnia, and EDS. Data collected during ARIC visit 4 and the SHHS was used for this analysis (1550 individuals of European ancestry with sleep and genetic data).

#### Bogalusa Heart Study

The BHS is a community-based prospective cohort study of the natural history and risk factors of cardiovascular disease among individuals in Bogalusa, Louisiana and has been described in detail previously [26]. Approximately two-thirds of individuals are White (65%) and one-third are Black (35%) and were aged 4-38 years old at baseline in 1972. Several follow-up visits were conducted every 2–3 years between baseline and the present. In 2013-2016 (BHS Biceps), comprehensive sleep questionnaires were administered to 1298 individuals. Among individuals with sleep data, 1078 also had genetic data.

#### Ethics statement

The HCHS/SOL was approved by the institutional review boards (IRBs) at each field center, where all participants gave written informed consent, and by the Non-Biomedical IRB at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill to the HCHS/SOL Data Coordinating Center. All IRBs approving the HCHS/SOL study are: Non-Biomedical IRB at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC; Einstein IRB at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine of Yeshiva University, Bronx, NY; IRB at Office for the Protection of Research Subjects (OPRS), University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago, IL; Human Subject Research Office, University of Miami, Miami, FL; and Institutional Review Board of San Diego State University, San Diego, CA.

For MESA, the UCLA IRB approved the field center activities. All MESA participants provided written informed consent, and the study was approved by the IRBs at The Lundquist Institute (formerly Los Angeles BioMedical Research Institute) at Harbor-UCLA Medical Center, University of Washington, Wake Forest School of Medicine, Northwestern University, University of Minnesota, Columbia University, and Johns Hopkins University.

For ARIC, written informed consent was provided by all study participants and the study design and methods were approved by IRBs at each of the collaborating medical institutions: University of Mississippi Medical Center Institutional Review Board (Jackson Field Center); Wake Forest University Health Sciences Institutional Review Board (Forsyth County Field Center); University of Minnesota Institutional Review Board (Minnesota Field Center); and Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health Institutional Review Board (Washington County Field Center).

For BHS, all participants gave written, informed consent prior to data collection and study procedures were approved by the Tulane University Health Sciences Institutional Review Board.

All methods and analyses were carried out in accordance with human subject research guidelines and regulations. This work was approved by the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center Committee on Clinical Investigations.

#### UKB PRS

We developed PRSs for the following five sleep phenotypes: sleep duration, short sleep, long sleep, insomnia and daytime sleepiness (Figure 1). For sleep duration, short sleep and long sleep we used results from a GWAS of nearly 450 000 individuals of European ancestry from UKB which ascertained sleep duration using the single question “About how many hours of sleep do you get in every 24h?” and defined short sleep as <7 hours and long sleep as ≥9 hours [13] (Supplemental Table 1). Similarly, we used results from other large GWAS within UKB for insomnia [14] and daytime sleepiness [15], which defined insomnia based on the single question “Do you have trouble falling asleep at night or do you wake up in the middle of the night?” and EDS based on the single question “How likely are you to doze off or fall asleep during the daytime when you don’t mean to?” (Supplemental Table 1). Based on the GWAS estimates from the respective study for each sleep phenotype, we inferred posterior effect sizes of variants using PRS-CS [34], with the following settings: 1000 Genomes European panel as the reference panel, HapMap variants lifted over to hg38 as the target data, and all other parameters at the default settings. The PRS weights are then the computed posterior effect estimates. Throughout, PRSs for each sleep phenotype among participants in each study were constructed using PLINK—score [35,36] or PRSice [37] without clumping or thresholding. For analysis, PRS were scaled in each study so estimates for associations were per 1 SD increase in the PRS.

#### MVP PRS

To compare with the PRS based on UKB data, we also constructed PRS based on recently published GWAS of sleep phenotypes using data from the MVP [16,17] (Figure 1). For short and long sleep, an MVP GWAS ascertained sleep duration using the single question “How many hours do you usually sleep each day (24-h period)?” and defined short sleep as ≤5 hours and long sleep as ≥10 hours [16] (Supplemental Table 1). This study stratified White and Black populations defined by patterns of genetic ancestry, referred to as EUR and AFR. In another GWAS of over 2000 traits in MVP, ICD codes were used to define insomnia and a single question about “feeling excessively sleepy during the day (does not include regular naps)” was used to define EDS [17] (Supplemental Table 1). GWAS summary statistics were available from four groups: EUR, AFR, AMR (primarily Hispanic ancestries), and EAS (primarily Asian ancestries). Given the multiethnic nature of the MVP data, we utilized two methods to construct PRS. First, we used PRS-CS [34] applied on the summary statistics from the EUR group only (the group with the largest sample size; using the same approach as before). Second, we used PRS-CSx [38] with the following settings: 1000 Genomes European, African, Asian, or Admixed American as reference panels corresponding to the MVP group available, same target data as before, and all other parameters at the default settings. Ancestry-specific posterior effect estimates were then used as ancestry-specific PRS weights. Ancestry-specific scaled MVP PRS-CSx were also summed to create a single multiethnic PRS.

#### UKB and MVP combined PRS

We combined PRS across the UKB and MVP GWAS using three methods. First, we meta-analyzed GWAS summary statistics from White individuals from both studies using GWAMA v.2.2.2, with parameters left at their default settings. We used PRS-CS to develop a PRS. Second, we used simple summation to combine the scaled UKB PRS and scaled MVP PRS-CS EUR PRS. Third, we used simple summation to combine the scaled UKB PRS and the scaled MVP EUR ancestry-specific PRS extracted from the PRS-CSx analysis. The latter (PRS-CSx European ancestry) may perform better than the first (PRS-CS EUR) because it was developed while borrowing information from the other available ancestry groups. For analysis, all secondary PRSs, including PRS summations, were scaled in each study so estimates for association were per 1 SD increase in the PRS.

### Statistical analysis

Each cohort used logistic or linear regression to estimate associations between the sleep PRSs and corresponding sleep phenotypes adjusting analyses for age, sex, center, and the first five (HCHS/SOL and MESA) or 10 (ARIC and BHS) ancestral PCs. BHS models were also adjusted for race (White, Black) and HCHS/SOL models incorporated sampling weights to account for its two-stage sampling design. Analyses further adjusted for body mass index (BMI), which is often included in analyses of sleep conditions [39], and stratification by sex were also considered to qualitatively assess robustness of results (i.e. no formal criteria for change in estimates was defined). Results from study-specific analyses were meta-analyzed using a fixed effects inverse-variance weighted approach. For PRS-sleep definitions estimates with evidence of heterogeneity across studies (p_{het} < 0.05), results from random effects meta-analyses are also reported.

To evaluate various sleep PRS and definitions, we first considered which associations were statistically significant at p-values <0.05 in meta-analyses, particularly definitions with the lowest p-value of each sleep phenotype. Among definitions significantly associated with sleep PRS, we next considered which definitions were most consistent across studies (i.e. highest p-value for heterogeneity). Finally, we considered sample size to ensure that definitions would not result in too few cases for reliable analyses.

We estimated the variance explained by each UKB PRS (on top of the other covariates in the model) and its respective consensus sleep phenotype definition using the r2_var function in the r2redux R package [40]. As it is recommended to use at least 2000 individuals in such analysis, it was performed using unrelated individuals from HCHS/SOL only.

To further substantiate the sleep definitions highlighted from the main association analyses of sleep PRSs with sleep phenotypes based on significance, consistency and sample size, we conducted secondary analyses of sleep phenotypes with the other complex and age-related traits, namely the DSST and hypertension. The DSST is a cognitive test in which participants replace a pattern of numbers with symbols based on a key [41]. Scores represent the number of correct digit-symbol pairs completed in 90 seconds (HCHS/SOL and ARIC) or 120 seconds (MESA and BHS), and scores for each study were then standardized using means and standard deviations (SDs). Hypertension was defined as systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140, diastolic blood pressure (DBP) ≥90 or use of hypertension medication. Study-specific analyses were conducted using “glm” (for MESA, ARIC, and BHS) and “surveyglm” (for HCHS/SOL) and meta-analyses were performed using “meta” in R [42].

Another limitation of our study was that we were limited to evaluating the sleep questions and scales available in the HCHS/SOL, MESA, ARIC, and BHS so alternative questions and scales (e.g. the Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System PROMIS sleep scale or ISI) should be evaluated in other cohorts with such data. Although our study included four sleep phenotypes and several definitions per phenotype, we did not correct p-values for multiple comparisons as the tests were not independent. Indeed, many of the definitions considered for a particular sleep phenotype have some overlap and are not fully distinct (e.g. many individuals defined as long sleepers based on sleep duration >9 or ≥9 are the same). The similarity of thresholds used in sleep phenotype definitions was necessitated by differing questions across studies (e.g. sleep duration >9 and ≥9 were both considered because some cohorts ascertain sleep duration in increments of whole hours while other cohorts ascertain more precise partial hours). Moreover, we treated each phenotype as a separate analysis as has been done for other potentially correlated phenotypes (e.g. FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC for pulmonary function). Therefore, we utilized a nominal significance level (p < .05) and focused on comparing associations within each phenotype. However, it is also important to note that given the similarity of several sleep definitions within sleep phenotypes, associations were often similar across thresholds (i.e. similar estimates and overlapping 95% CIs) and had we corrected for multiple comparisons fewer associations would meet statistical significance criteria. Further, it is possible that some heterogeneity in results across definitions for a particular sleep phenotype may reflect to some degree differences in the proportion of cases meeting that criterion across studies rather than genetic vulnerability alone. For example, the percent of individuals classified as cases for short sleep ≤6 hours did not seem to vary greatly in HCHS/SOL, MESA and ARIC (7.7%–9.9%), but was higher in BHS (27.1%) and the percent of individuals classified as cases for long sleep ≥9 hours was similar in HCHS/SOL and MESA (23.4%–24.4%) but higher than ARIC and BHS (6.2-6.8%, Table 2). Additionally, it is important to note that the more restrictive definitions (e.g. short sleep ≤5 hours or long sleep ≥10 hours) not only result in a smaller number of cases but also likely reflect more extreme phenotypes. For these reasons, we compared associations between sleep PRS and sleep phenotypes based on several factors including statistical significance, consistency across studies, and sample sizes.

Finally, previous research has shown high correlation between PRS derived from a variety of genotyping methods (i.e. differing arrays + imputation vs WGS) [51]. Although differences in genotyping methods can impact PRS based on a large number of INDELS or when using PRS for risk stratification [51], our study did neither. Further, while differences in pre-phasing and imputation tools across studies can impact scores at an individual level, PRS variability is minimal (<5 percentile rank change) and therefore does not usually impact interpretability and reproducibility at the population level [52]. Therefore, we do not believe differences in genotyping methods across the cohorts used in our study would lead to any large-scale bias.

In general, harmonizing data can be challenging given the wide-array of field-specific situations and potential pitfalls including access to individual-level data, differences in data content and quality, balancing internal and external validity, and infrastructure to harmonize data [53,54]. Despite such challenges, numerous initiatives in the field of epidemiology have been established to harmonize data for a wide-variety of exposures and outcomes [54]. Here we sought to use the PRS as another tool to evaluate consensus definitions across studies. Although the low estimated percent variance explained by sleep PRS across sleep measures is expected given that PRS typically have r^{2} <1% across most phenotypes [55], it does indicate that PRS alone are insufficient to establish clinical definitions. Nevertheless, sleep PRS can complement demographic and environmental information to comprehensively evaluate sleep outcomes and help highlight which sleep definitions are associated with sleep genetics. Given the differences in sleep questions and potential responses across studies our analysis focused on binary definitions of sleep rather than continuous measures. For example, since WHIIRS was based on five questions in some studies and three questions in others, we focused on analyzing high versus low scores rather than the continuous metric. This approach helped to evaluate consensus definitions of sleep measures even when questions and potential responses differed slightly. Additionally, previous studies of sleep, including the GWAS used to develop PRS, have often utilized binary sleep definitions since investigators are often trying to characterize whether individuals have a sleep disorder or not, and the factors that predict that dichotomization. However, when the research goal is to study whether a sleep trait has a biological relationship with a gene or biomarker then continuous measures of sleep may help capture further biological variation. To this end, we did note stronger associations between sleep PRS and continuous sleep measures compared to binary sleep measures.
